steps.body: To compare irrationals and rationals fairly, convert everything to decimals first. Notation (radicals, fractions, decimals) can trick the eye — decimals put every number on equal footing for comparison.

misorderFeedback.feedback: √2 ≈ 1.414 is LESS than 1.5 = 3/2, even though a fraction can look 'plainer' — compare the decimals, not the notation.
√3 ≈ 1.732 is LESS than 1.8 — convert to decimals to compare fairly.

widget.missFeedback: Not quite — convert every value to a decimal, then compare.

steps.body: To estimate an expression like π², use a rational approximation for π — like 3.14 — and compute: 3.14² ≈ 9.86, so π² ≈ 9.86. That estimate is close to, but never exactly, the true (irrational) value of π² itself.
Compare a root to a decimal.
explanationVariants: Converting √5 to a decimal (≈2.236) makes the comparison to 2.1 direct.

options.label: √5, since √5 ≈ 2.236 > 2.1
options.feedback: Right — convert to a decimal and compare directly.

options.label: 2.1, since it has more decimal digits shown
options.feedback: How many digits are WRITTEN doesn't decide size — √5 ≈ 2.236 is genuinely bigger than 2.1.

options.label: Can't compare a root to a decimal
options.feedback: You can — convert the root to its decimal approximation and compare like any two numbers.

widget.lowFeedback: Too low — try squaring a number a bit bigger than 3.
widget.highFeedback: Too high — π is only a little more than 3, so π² shouldn't be too far past 9 or 10.
widget.successFeedback: π² ≈ 9.87 — close to 10, since π is just a bit more than 3, and 3² = 9.

predict.prompt: π is a bit more than 3. Where will π² land?
predict.reveal: Squaring a-bit-more-than-3 gives a-bit-more-than-9 — the extra 0.14 pushes π² up near 10 but never past it.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents rns compare estimate.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for rns compare estimate must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines rns compare estimate.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: Both are close to π, but 22/7 is a famous slight OVER-estimate.

options.label: 22/7, since 22/7 ≈ 3.1429 is slightly more than π ≈ 3.1416
options.feedback: Right — 22/7 is a classic slight over-estimate of π.

options.label: π, since π is 'more precise' so must be bigger
options.feedback: Precision doesn't decide size — as decimals, 22/7 ≈ 3.1429 edges out π ≈ 3.1416.

options.label: They're exactly equal
options.feedback: 22/7 is only an approximation of π, not an exact match — they differ starting at the thousandths place.

options.label: Can't tell without a calculator
options.feedback: You can tell — 22/7 = 3.142857… and π = 3.141592… — compare digit by digit.

explanationVariants: Squaring a square root undoes it exactly: √3 × √3 = 3.
By definition, √3 is the number that squares to 3 — so multiplying it by itself returns exactly 3.

options.label: 3, exactly
options.feedback: Right — squaring a square root always returns the original number exactly.

options.label: ≈1.732, since that's what √3 rounds to
options.feedback: That's √3 itself, not √3 times √3 — the product is exactly 3.

options.label: 9, since 3² = 9
options.feedback: That squares the number 3, not √3 — here we're multiplying √3 by itself, which gives 3.

options.label: Irrational, since √3 is irrational
options.feedback: An irrational number times itself CAN be rational — here, √3 × √3 = 3 exactly, a whole number.

explanationVariants: √8 ≈ 2.828, then 2.9, then 3, then √10 ≈ 3.162 — converting to decimals lines them all up.
√8 < 2.9 since 2.828 < 2.9, and √10 > 3 since 10 > 9 = 3² — decimals settle both comparisons.

steps.body: Convert to decimals to compare fairly; approximate irrational expressions with rational stand-ins.
takeaways: Convert radicals and fractions to decimals before comparing them.
Rational approximations (like 3.14 or 22/7) estimate irrational expressions.
Squaring a square root returns the original number exactly.
